opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so the rabbit example comes from our work on planning in poetry, and it's a nice way to see how a concept moves through the model. If you give the model the first line of a rhyming couplet, something like "He saw a carrot and had to grab it," you might expect it to just improvise word by word and then scramble for a rhyme at the end. What we actually found, using attribution graphs, is that on the newline token, before it has written a single word of the second line, the model is already representing candidate rhyming words. "Rabbit" is one of them, and "habit" shows up too.

How do I think about how that spreads across layers? A concept like rabbit isn't sitting in one neuron at one spot. In the early layers, what you see is mostly about the literal tokens: the word "grab it," the "-abbit" sound, the fact that we're in a poem with a rhyme scheme. As you go through the middle layers, those pieces combine into more abstract features. You get something like "I need a word that rhymes with 'it' or 'abbit,'" and separately the semantic context of carrots and grabbing pulls toward animals that eat carrots. Where those two pressures meet, the rabbit feature lights up. It's really a feature that's been composed from several earlier ones.

Then that planned word shapes everything that comes after. The model writes a line like "His hunger was like a starving rabbit," and the earlier words in the line are chosen to set up landing on "rabbit." The test that convinced us it was a real plan was intervention: if you go in and suppress the rabbit feature at that planning position, the model writes a different line ending in "habit." If you inject a totally different concept, like "green," it rewrites the line to end on "green," even though that breaks the rhyme. So the representation isn't a passive byproduct. It's causally steering the generation.

My general mental model is that concepts are distributed across many features and many layers, and they're constantly being read from and written to the residual stream. What interpretability tools let us do is trace those paths: which features contributed to rabbit, and which downstream features rabbit then influences. It's messy and only a partial picture. Our graphs explain some fraction of the computation, not all of it. But it's a lot more structured than "it just predicts the next token," and the rabbit case is one of the clearest windows we have into the model actually thinking ahead.

r001.rationale: The response says suppressing the rabbit feature at the planning position changes the ending, but does not describe removing an early representation or later stages merely reinforcing it.

r002.rationale: It does not say later layers can independently recreate rabbit after an earlier representation is removed.

r003.rationale: It describes features combining through middle layers into a rabbit feature and says concepts are distributed across many features and layers, communicating that computation is spread across successive layers.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so the first thing to say is that "rabbit" isn't really stored in one place. When we use our interpretability tools, what we do is take the model's activations at a given layer and decompose them into these features, which you can think of as the model's internal concepts. And what you find is that there's a whole family of features that relate to rabbits. Early on, there are features that are much more tied to the actual tokens, so something that fires on the word "rabbit" or "bunny" or "hare." Then as you go deeper into the model, you get features that are more abstract, that fire on the concept of a rabbit regardless of how it's written, regardless of the language even. And then later still, you get features that are about what the model wants to do with that concept, like "I'm about to say a word that rhymes with rabbit" or "this is an animal that would make sense in this sentence."

So the way I think about it is that each layer is doing a little bit of processing, and the residual stream is kind of a shared workspace. Layer one reads the token, writes "this is the word rabbit." A few layers later, something reads that and writes "we're talking about an animal, small, furry." And the attribution graphs we build let you actually trace that: you can see this feature at layer five caused that feature at layer twelve, which caused the output.

The example I love is the poetry one. We gave the model a line ending in a rhyme, and it was planning the word "rabbit" at the newline, before it had written any of the second line. There's a feature there that is essentially "rabbit, as a candidate for the end of this line." And then the model writes the whole line with that goal in mind. If you suppress that feature, it picks a different rhyme and rewrites the line to fit. So the concept isn't just propagating forward passively, it's being used, it's steering what comes next. That's what makes it feel less like a lookup table and more like a computation.

r001.rationale: The response says suppressing a rhyme-related feature changes the chosen rhyme, but does not describe removing an early rabbit representation or later stages merely reinforcing it.

r002.rationale: It does not state that later layers can independently produce a rabbit representation after an earlier one is removed.

r003.rationale: The response describes incremental processing across layers, but does not communicate that a single computation is distributed across successive MLP layers.

astra-6.text:
I think it helps to distinguish a concept from a particular neuron. You might imagine that somewhere in the model there’s a rabbit neuron, and once that activates, the model knows it’s talking about a rabbit. But a concept can be represented by a pattern of activity across many neurons, and that pattern can change from layer to layer.

So, if you’re processing a sentence about a rabbit, one layer might represent information about the word itself. Later layers might bring in properties of the animal, or its role in the sentence, or information relevant to predicting what comes next. Those aren’t necessarily clean, discrete stages; they’re interacting computations.

The interesting question is how to trace that information. If we can detect something related to rabbits at several layers, that doesn’t by itself tell us how the model uses it. We’d want to intervene on those representations and see what changes downstream. That helps distinguish information that’s merely present from information that actually contributes to the model’s behavior.

r001.rationale: It discusses changing representations across layers but does not say removing an early rabbit representation suppresses later ones through reinforcement.

r002.rationale: It does not state that later layers can independently produce a rabbit representation after an earlier one is removed.

r003.rationale: It describes interacting computations across layers but does not state that a single computation can be distributed across successive MLP layers.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the first thing to be careful about is that there probably isn’t one place in the model where the concept of a rabbit lives. It’s represented across many activations, and that representation changes as you go through the layers.

Early on, the model might be dealing with the token itself and fairly local context. Later layers can bring in information that helps distinguish, say, a pet rabbit from a rabbit in a story or the phrase “down the rabbit hole.” But that’s a rough intuition, not a clean sequence where each layer has one identifiable job.

One way to investigate this is to look for features associated with rabbits at different layers, then intervene on those features and see what changes. Can you make the model more likely to talk about rabbits? Does the intervention affect related ideas? That gives you stronger evidence than simply finding an activation that lights up when the word “rabbit” appears. The interesting question is how those representations influence what the model does next.

r001.rationale: The response says rabbit representations change across layers, but does not describe removing an early representation suppressing later ones or say later stages merely reinforce it.

r002.rationale: It does not state that later layers can independently produce a rabbit representation after an earlier one is removed.

r003.rationale: It discusses representations across layers, but does not state that a single computation can be distributed across successive MLP layers.
